and it magnifies the wisdom and power of God that though they crucified him, and thought thereby to have put him under an indelible mark of infamy, yet God had glorified him, and the indignities they had done him served as a foil to his lustre. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That he has glorified him to such a degree as to make him <hi type="italic">both Lord and Christ:</hi> these signify the same; he is <hi type="italic">Lord of all,</hi> and he is not a usurper, but is <hi type="italic">Christ, anointed</hi> to be so. He is <hi type="italic">one Lord to the Gentiles,</hi> who had had lords many; and <hi type="italic">to the Jews he is Messiah,</hi> which includes all his offices. He is <hi type="italic">the king Messiah,</hi> as the Chaldee paraphrast calls him; or, as the angel to Daniel, <hi type="italic">Messiah the prince,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.9.25">Dan. ix. 25</reference>. This is the great truth of the gospel which we are to believe, <hi type="italic">that that same Jesus,</hi> the very same <hi type="italic">that was crucified at Jerusalem,</hi> is he to whom we owe allegiance, and from whom we are to expect protection, as <hi type="italic">Lord and Christ.</hi>
entries.71caed783f72aa7757ccf85efc18bd13e7eb059b: <div eID="gen28954" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Peter's Sermon at Jerusalem.</title> <div sID="gen28955" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">37</hi> Now when they heard <hi type="italic">this,</hi> they were pricked in their heart, and said unto Peter and to the rest of the apostles, Men <hi type="italic">and</hi> brethren, what shall we do? <hi type="super">38</hi> Then Peter said unto them, Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost. <hi type="super">39</hi> For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, <hi type="italic">even</hi> as many as the Lord our God shall call. <hi type="super">40</hi> And with many other words did he testify and exhort, saying, Save yourselves from this untoward generation. <hi type="super">41</hi> Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added <hi type="italic">unto them</hi> about three thousand souls. <div eID="gen28955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28956" type="x-p"/> We have seen the wonderful effect of the pouring out of the Spirit, in its influence upon the preachers of the gospel. Peter, in all his life, never spoke at the rate that he had done now, with such fulness, perspicuity, and power. We are now to see another blessed fruit of the pouring out of the Spirit in its influence upon the hearers of the gospel. From the first delivery of that divine message, it appeared that there was a divine power going along with it, and <hi type="italic">it was mighty, through God,</hi> to do wonders: thousands were immediately brought by it to the <hi type="italic">obedience of faith;</hi> it was <hi type="italic">the rod of God's strength sent out of Zion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.2-Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 2, 3</reference>. We have here the first-fruits of that vast harvest of souls which by it were gathered in to Jesus Christ. Come and see, in these verses, the exalted Redeemer riding forth, in these chariots of salvation, <hi type="italic">conquering and to conquer,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.6.2">Rev. vi. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen28956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28957" type="x-p"/> In these verses we find the word of God the means of beginning and carrying on a good work of grace in the hearts of many, <hi type="italic">the Spirit of the Lord working by it.</hi> Let us see the method of it. <div eID="gen28957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28958" type="x-p"/> I. They were startled, and convinced, and put upon a serious enquiry, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.37">v. 37</reference>. <hi type="italic">When they heard,</hi> or <hi type="italic">having heard,</hi> having patiently heard Peter out, and not given him the interruption they had been used to give to Christ in his discourses (this was one good point gained, that they were become attentive to the word), <hi type="italic">they were pricked to the heart,</hi> or <hi type="italic">in the heart,</hi> and, under a deep concern and perplexity, applied themselves to the preachers with this question, <hi type="italic">What shall we do?</hi> It was very strange that such impressions should be made upon such hard hearts all of a sudden. They were Jews, bred up in the opinion of the sufficiency of their religion to save them, had lately seen this Jesus crucified in weakness and disgrace, and were told by their rulers that he was a deceiver. Peter had charged them with having a hand, a <hi type="italic">wicked hand,</hi> in his death, which was likely to have exasperated them against him; yet, when they heard this plain scriptural sermon, they were much affected with it. <div eID="gen28958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28959" type="x-p"/> 1. It put them in pain: <hi type="italic">They were pricked in their hearts.</hi> We read of those that were <hi type="italic">cut to the heart</hi> with indignation at the preacher (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.54">ch. vii. 54</reference>), but these were <hi type="italic">pricked to the heart</hi> with indignation at themselves for having been accessory to the death of Christ. Peter, charging it upon them, awakened their consciences, touched them to the quick, and the reflection they now made upon it was as <hi type="italic">a sword in their bones,</hi> it pierced them as they had pierced Christ. Note, Sinners, when their eyes are opened, cannot but be <hi type="italic">pricked to the heart</hi> for sin, cannot but experience an inward uneasiness; this is having the <hi type="italic">heart rent</hi> (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.13">Joel ii. 13</reference>), <hi type="italic">a broken and contrite heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.51.17">Ps. li. 17</reference>. Those that are truly sorry for their sins, and ashamed of them, and afraid of the consequences of them, are <hi type="italic">pricked to the heart.</hi> A prick in the heart is mortal, and under those commotions (says Paul) I died, <reference osisRef="Rom.7.9">Rom. vii. 9</reference>. "All my good opinion of myself and confidence in myself failed me." <div eID="gen28959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28960" type="x-p"/> 2. It put them upon enquiry. <hi type="italic">Our of the abundance of the heart,</hi> thus pricked, <hi type="italic">the mouth spoke.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen28960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28961" type="x-p"/> (1.) To whom they thus addressed themselves: <hi type="italic">To Peter and to the rest of the apostles,</hi> some to one and some to another; to them they opened their case; by them they had been convinced, and therefore by them they expect to be counselled and comforted. They do not appeal from them to the scribes and Pharisees, to justify them against the apostles' charge, but apply to them, as owning the charge, and referring the case to them. They call them <hi type="italic">men</hi> and <hi type="italic">brethren,</hi> as Peter had called them (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.29">v. 29</reference>): it is a style of friendship and love, rather than a title of honour: "You are men, look upon us with humanity; you are brethren, look upon us with brotherly love." Note, Ministers are spiritual physicians; they should be advised with by those whose consciences are wounded; and it is good for people to be free and familiar with those ministers, as men and their brethren, who deal for their souls as for their own. <div eID="gen28961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28962" type="x-p"/> (2.) What the address is: <hi type="italic">What shall we do?</hi> [1.] They speak as men at a stand, that did not know what to do; in a perfect surprise: "<hi type="italic">Is that Jesus</hi> whom we have crucified both <hi type="italic">Lord and Christ?</hi> Then what will become of us who crucified him? We are all undone!" Note, No way of being happy but by seeing ourselves miserable. When we find ourselves in danger of being lost for ever, there is hope of our being made for ever, and not till then. [2.] They speak as men at a point, that were resolved to do any thing they should be directed to immediately; they are not for taking time to consider, nor for adjourning the prosecution of their convictions to a more convenient season, but desire now to be told what they must do to escape the misery they were liable to. Note, those that are convinced of sin would gladly know the way to peace and pardon, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.6">ch. ix. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.16.30">xvi. 30</reference>. <div eID="gen28962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28963" type="x-p"/> II. Peter and the other apostles direct them in short what they must do, and what in so doing they might expect, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.38-Acts.2.39">v. 38, 39</reference>. Sinners convinced must be encouraged; and that which is broken must be bound up (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.16">Ezek. xxxiv. 16</reference>); they must be told that though their case is sad it is not desperate, there is hope for them. <div eID="gen28963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28964" type="x-p"/> 1. He here shows them the course they must take. (1.) <hi type="italic">Repent;</hi> this is a plank after shipwreck. "Let the sense of this horrid guilt which you have brought upon yourselves by putting Christ to death awaken you to a penitent reflection upon all your other sins (as the demand of some one great debt brings to light all the debts of a poor bankrupt) and to bitter remorse and sorrow for them" This was the same duty that John the Baptist and Christ had preached, and now that the Spirit is poured out is it still insisted on: "<hi type="italic">Repent, repent;</hi> change your mind, change your way; admit an after-thought." (2.) <hi type="italic">Be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ;</hi> that is, "firmly believe the doctrine of Christ, and submit to his grace and government; and make an open solemn profession of this, and come under an engagement to abide by it, by submitting to the ordinance of baptism; be proselyted to Christ and to his holy religion, and renounce your infidelity." They must be baptized <hi type="italic">in the name of Jesus Christ.</hi> They did believe in the Father and the Holy Ghost speaking by the prophets; but they must also believe in the name of Jesus, that he is the Christ, the Messias promised to the fathers. "Take Jesus for your king, and by baptism swear allegiance to him; take him for your prophet, and hear him; take him for your priest, to make atonement for you," which seems peculiarly intended here; for they must be baptized <hi type="italic">in his name</hi> for the <hi type="italic">remission of sins</hi> upon the score of his righteousness. (3.) This is pressed upon each particular person: <hi type="italic">Every one of you.</hi> "Even those of you that have been the greatest sinners, if they repent and believe, are welcome to be baptized; and those who think they have been the greatest saints have yet need to repent, and believe, and be baptized. There is grace enough in Christ for every one of you, be you ever so many, and grace suited to the case of every one. Israel of old were baptized unto Moses in the camp, the whole body of the Israelites together, when they passed <hi type="italic">through the cloud</hi> and <hi type="italic">the sea</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.1-1Cor.10.2">1 Cor. x. 1, 2</reference>), for the covenant of peculiarity was national; but now <hi type="italic">every one of you</hi> distinctly must be <hi type="italic">baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus,</hi> and transact for himself in this great affair." See <reference osisRef="Col.1.28">Col. i. 28</reference>. <div eID="gen28964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28965" type="x-p"/> 2. He gives them encouragement to take this course:—(1.) "It shall be for <hi type="italic">the remission of sins.</hi> Repent of your sin, and it shall not be your ruin; be baptized into the faith of Christ, and in truth you shall be justified, which you could never be by the law of Moses. Aim at this, and depend upon Christ for it, and this you shall have. As the cup in the Lord's supper is the New Testament in the blood of Christ for the remission of sins, so baptism is in the name of Christ for the remission of sins. Be washed, and you shall be washed." (2.) "You shall <hi type="italic">receive the gift of the Holy Ghost</hi> as well as we; for it is designed for a general blessing: some of you shall receive these external gifts, and each of you, if you be sincere in your faith and repentance, shall receive his internal graces and comforts, shall be <hi type="italic">sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise.</hi>" Note, All that receive the remission of sins <hi type="italic">receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.</hi> All that are justified are sanctified. (3.) "Your children shall still have, as they have had, an interest in the covenant, and a title to the external seal of it. Come over to Christ, to receive those inestimable benefits; for the promise of the remission of sins, and the gift of the Holy Ghost, is <hi type="italic">to you and to your children,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Acts.2.39">v. 39</reference>. It was very express (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.3">Isa. xliv. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will pour my Spirit upon thy seed.</hi> And (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.21">Isa. lix. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">My Spirit and my word shall not depart from thy seed, and thy seed's seed.</hi> When God took Abraham into covenant, he said, <hi type="italic">I will be a God to thee, and to thy seed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.7">Gen. xvii. 7</reference>); and, accordingly, every Israelite had his son circumcised at eight days old. Now it is proper for an Israelite, when he is by baptism to come into a new dispensation of this covenant, to ask, "What must be done with my children? Must they be thrown out, or taken in with me?" "Taken in" (says Peter) "by all means; for the promise, that great promise of God's being to you a God, is as much to you and to your children now as ever it was." (4.) "Though the promise is still extended to your children as it has been, yet it is not, as it has been, confined to you and them, but the benefit of it is <hi type="italic">designed</hi> for <hi type="italic">all that are afar off;</hi>" we may add, <hi type="italic">and their children,</hi> for the blessing of Abraham comes upon the Gentiles, through Jesus Christ, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.14">Gal. iii. 14</reference>. The promise had long pertained to the Israelites (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.4">Rom. ix. 4</reference>); but now it is sent to <hi type="italic">those that are afar off,</hi> the remotest nations of the Gentiles, and <hi type="italic">every one</hi> of them too, <hi type="italic">all that are afar off.</hi> To this general the following limitation must refer, <hi type="italic">even as many of them,</hi> as many particular persons in each nation, <hi type="italic">as the Lord our God shall call</hi> effectually into the fellowship of Jesus Christ. Note, God can make his call to reach those that are ever so far off, and none come but those whom he calls. <div eID="gen28965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28966" type="x-p"/> III. These directions are followed with a needful caution (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.40">v. 40</reference>): <hi type="italic">With many other words,</hi> to the same purport, <hi type="italic">did he testify</hi> gospel truths, and exhort to gospel duties; now that the word began to work he followed it; he had said much in a little (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.38-Acts.2.39">v. 38, 39</reference>), and that which, one would think, included all, and yet he had more to say. When we have heard those words which have done our souls good, we cannot but wish to hear more, to hear many more such words. Among other things he said (and it should seem inculcated it), <hi type="italic">Save yourselves from this untoward generation. Be you free</hi> from them. The unbelieving Jews were an untoward generation, perverse and obstinate; they walked contrary to God and man (<reference osisRef="1Thess.2.15">1 Thess. ii. 15</reference>), wedded to sin and marked for ruin. Now as to them, 1. "Give diligence to save yourselves from their ruin, that you may not be involved in that, and may <hi type="italic">escape all those things</hi>" (as the Christians did): "<hi type="italic">Repent, and be baptized;</hi> and then you shall not be sharers in destruction with those with whom you have been sharers in sin." <hi type="italic">O gather not my soul with sinners.</hi> 2. "In order to this continue not with them in their sin, persist not with them in infidelity. <hi type="italic">Save yourselves,</hi> that is, separate yourselves, distinguish yourselves, from this <hi type="italic">untoward generation. Be not rebellious like this rebellious house;</hi> partake not with them in their sins, that you share not with them in their plagues." Note, To separate ourselves from wicked people is the only way to save ourselves from them; though we hereby expose ourselves to their rage and enmity, we really save ourselves from them; for, if we consider whither they are hastening, we shall see it is better to have the trouble of swimming against their stream than the danger of being carried down their stream. Those that repent of their sins, and give up themselves to Jesus Christ, must evidence their sincerity by breaking off all intimate society with wicked people. <hi type="italic">Depart from me, ye evil doers,</hi> is the language of one that determines to keep <hi type="italic">the commandments of his God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.115">Ps. cxix. 115</reference>. We must <hi type="italic">save ourselves</hi> from them, which denotes avoiding them with dread and holy fear, as we would save ourselves from an enemy that seeks to destroy us, or from a house infected with the plague. <div eID="gen28966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28967" type="x-p"/> IV. Here is the happy success and issue of this, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.41">v. 41</reference>. The Spirit wrought with the word, and wrought wonders by it. These same persons that had many of them been eye-witnesses of the death of Christ, and the prodigies that attended it, and were not wrought upon by them, were yet wrought upon by the preaching of the word, for it is this that is the <hi type="italic">power of God unto salvation.</hi> 1. They received the word; and <hi type="italic">then</hi> only the word does us good, when we do receive it, embrace it, and bid it welcome. They admitted the conviction of it, and accepted the offers of it. 2. They gladly received it. Herod <hi type="italic">heard</hi> the word gladly, but these gladly <hi type="italic">received</hi> it, were not only glad that they had it to receive, but glad that by the grace of God they were enabled to receive it, though it would be a humbling changing word to them, and would expose them to the enmity of their countrymen. 3. They were baptized; believing with the heart, they made confession with the mouth, and enrolled themselves among the disciples of Christ by that sacred rite and ceremony which he had instituted. And though Peter had said, "Be baptized in the name of <hi type="italic">the Lord Jesus</hi>" (because the doctrine of Christ was the present truth), yet we have reason to think that, in baptizing them, the whole form Christ prescribed was used, <hi type="italic">in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost.</hi> Note, Those that receive the Christian covenant ought to receive the Christian baptism. 4. Hereby there were added to the disciples to the number of about <hi type="italic">three thousand souls that same day.</hi> All those that had received the Holy Ghost had their tongues at work to preach, and their hands at work to baptize; for it was time to be busy, when such a harvest was to be gathered in. The conversion of these three thousand with these words was a <hi type="italic">greater work</hi> than the feeding of four or five thousand with a few loaves. Now Israel began to multiply after the death of our Joseph. They are said to be <hi type="italic">three thousand souls</hi> (which word is generally used for persons when women and children are included with men, as <reference osisRef="Gen.14.21">Gen. xiv. 21</reference>, <hi type="italic">margin, Give me the souls;</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.46.27">Gen. xlvi. 27</reference>, <hi type="italic">seventy souls</hi>), which intimates that those that were here baptized were not so many men, but so many heads of families as, with their children and servants baptized, might make up <hi type="italic">three thousand souls.</hi> These were <hi type="italic">added to them.</hi> Note, Those who are joined to Christ are added to the disciples of Christ, and join with them. When we take God for our God, we must take his people to be our people.
entries.c6a08d07a9790f0f87a131cae682597cc4bd98c3: <div eID="gen28967" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Fellowship of the Disciples.</title> <div sID="gen28968" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">42</hi> And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers. <hi type="super">43</hi> And fear came upon every soul: and many wonders and signs were done by the apostles. <hi type="super">44</hi> And all that believed were together, and had all things common; <hi type="super">45</hi> And sold their possessions and goods, and parted them to all <hi type="italic">men,</hi> as every man had need. <hi type="super">46</hi> And they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart, 47 Praising God, and having favour with all the people. And the Lord added to the church daily such as should be saved. <div eID="gen28968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28969" type="x-p"/> We often speak of the primitive church, and appeal to it, and to the history of it; in these verses we have the history of the <hi type="italic">truly primitive church,</hi> of the <hi type="italic">first days</hi> of it, its state of infancy indeed, but, like that, the state of its greatest <hi type="italic">innocence.</hi> <div eID="gen28969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28970" type="x-p"/> I. They kept close to holy ordinances, and abounded in all instances of piety and devotion, for Christianity, admitted in the power of it, will dispose the soul to communion with God in all those ways wherein he has appointed us to meet him and promised to meet us. <div eID="gen28970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28971" type="x-p"/> 1. They were diligent and constant inn their attendance upon the <hi type="italic">preaching of the word.</hi> They <hi type="italic">continued in the apostles' doctrine,</hi> and never disowned nor deserted it; or, as it may be read, <hi type="italic">they continued constant to the apostles' teaching</hi> or <hi type="italic">instruction;</hi> by <hi type="italic">baptism</hi> they were discipled to be taught, and they were willing to be taught. Note, Those who have given up their names to Christ must make conscience of hearing his word; for thereby we give honour to him, and build up ourselves in our most holy faith. <div eID="gen28971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28972" type="x-p"/> 2. They kept up the <hi type="italic">communion of saints.</hi> They continued <hi type="italic">in fellowship</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.42">v. 42</reference>), and <hi type="italic">continued daily with one accord in the temple,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.46">v. 46</reference>. They not only had a mutual affection to each other, but a great deal of mutual conversation with each other; they were much together. When they withdrew from <hi type="italic">the untoward</hi> generation, they did not turn hermits, but were very intimate with one another, and took all occasions to meet; wherever you saw one disciple, you would see more, like <hi type="italic">birds of a feather.</hi> See how these Christians love one another. They were concerned for one another, sympathized with one another, and heartily espoused one another's interests. They had fellowship with one another in religious worship. They met <hi type="italic">in the temple:</hi> there was their rendezvous; for joint-fellowship with God is the best fellowship we can have with one another, <reference osisRef="1John.1.3">1 John i. 3</reference>. Observe, (1.) They were daily in the temple, not only on the days of the sabbaths and solemn feasts, but on other days, every day. Worshipping God is to be our daily work, and, where there is opportunity, the oftener it is done publicly the better. God loves the gates of Zion, and so must we. (2.) They were <hi type="italic">with one accord;</hi> not only no discord nor strife, but a great deal of holy love among them; and they heartily joined in their public services. Though they met with the Jews in the courts of the temple, yet the Christians kept together by themselves, and were unanimous in their separate devotions. <div eID="gen28972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28973" type="x-p"/> 3. They frequently joined in the ordinance of the Lord's supper. They continued <hi type="italic">in the breaking of bread,</hi> in celebrating that memorial of their Master's death, as those that were not ashamed to own their relation to, and their dependence upon, Christ and him crucified. They could not forget the death of Christ, yet they kept up this memorial of it, and made it their constant practice, because it was an institution of Christ, to be transmitted to the succeeding ages of the church. They broke bread <hi type="italic">from house to house;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kat oikon</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">house by house;</hi> they did not think fit to celebrate the eucharist in the temple, for that was peculiar to the Christian institutes, and therefore they administered that ordinance in private houses, choosing such houses of the converted Christians as were convenient, to which the neighbours resorted; and they went from one to another of these little synagogues or domestic chapels, houses that had churches in them, and there celebrated the eucharist with those that usually met there to worship God. <div eID="gen28973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28974" type="x-p"/> 4. They continued <hi type="italic">in prayers. After</hi> the Spirit was poured out, as well as before, while they were waiting for him, they continued instant in prayer; for prayer will never be superseded till it comes to be swallowed up in everlasting praise. <hi type="italic">Breaking of bread</hi> comes in between the <hi type="italic">work</hi> and <hi type="italic">prayer,</hi> for it has reference to both, and is a help to both. The Lord's supper is a sermon to the eye, and a confirmation of God's word to us; and it is an encouragement to our prayers, and a solemn expression of the ascent of our souls to God. <div eID="gen28974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28975" type="x-p"/> 5. They abounded in thanksgiving; were continually <hi type="italic">praising God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.47">v. 47</reference>. This should have a part in every prayer, and not be crowded into a corner. Those that have received the gift of the Holy Ghost will be much in praise. <div eID="gen28975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28976" type="x-p"/> II. They were loving one to another, and very kind; their charity was as eminent as their piety, and their joining together in holy ordinances knit their hearts to each other, and very much endeared them to one another. <div eID="gen28976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28977" type="x-p"/> 1. They had frequent meetings for Christian converse (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.44">v. 44</reference>): <hi type="italic">All that believed were together;</hi> not all those thousands in one place (this was impracticable); but, as Dr. Lightfoot explains it, they kept together in several companies or congregations, according as their languages, nations, or other associations, brought them and kept them together. And thus joining together, because it was apart from those that believed not, and because it was in the same profession and practice of the duties of religion, they are said to be together, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">epi to auto</hi></hi>. They associated together, and so both expressed and increased their mutual love. <div eID="gen28977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28978" type="x-p"/> 2. They had <hi type="italic">all things common;</hi> perhaps they had common tables (as the Spartans of old), for familiarity, temperance and freedom of conversation; they <hi type="italic">ate together,</hi> that those who had much might have the less, and so be kept from the temptations of abundance; and they who had little might have the more, and so be kept from the temptations of want and poverty. Or, There was such a concern for one another, and such a readiness to help one another as there was occasion, that it might be said, They had <hi type="italic">all things common,</hi> according to the law of friendship; one wanted not what another had; for he might have it for the asking. <div eID="gen28978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28979" type="x-p"/> 3. They were very cheerful, and very generous in the use of what they had. Besides the religion that was in their sacred feasts (their <hi type="italic">breaking bread from house to house</hi>) a great deal of it appeared in their common meals; they did <hi type="italic">eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart.</hi> They brought the comforts of <hi type="italic">God's table</hi> along with them to <hi type="italic">their own,</hi> which had two good effects upon them:—(1.) It made them very pleasant, and enlarged their hearts with holy joy; they did eat their bread with joy, and <hi type="italic">drank their wine with a merry heart,</hi> as knowing that <hi type="italic">God now accepted their works.</hi> None have such cause to be cheerful as good Christians have; it is a pity but that they should always have hearts to be so. (2.) It made them very liberal to their poor brethren, and enlarged their hearts in charity. They did <hi type="italic">eat their meat with singleness of heart,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">en apheloteti kardias</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">with liberality of heart;</hi> so some: they did not eat their morsels alone, but bade the poor welcome to their table, not grudgingly, but with all the hearty freedom imaginable. Note, It becomes Christians to be open-hearted and open-handed, and in every good work to sow plentifully, as those on whom God hath sown plentifully, and who hope to reap so. <div eID="gen28979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28980" type="x-p"/> 4. They raised a fund for charity (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.45">v. 45</reference>): They <hi type="italic">sold their possessions and goods;</hi> some sold their lands and houses, others their stocks and the furniture of their houses, and <hi type="italic">parted</hi> the money to their brethren, <hi type="italic">as every man had need.</hi> This was to destroy, not property (as Mr. Baxter says), but selfishness. Herein, probably, they had an eye to the command which Christ gave to the rich man, as a test of his sincerity, <hi type="italic">Sell that thou hast, and give to the poor.</hi> Not that this was intended for an example to be a constant binding rule, as if all Christians in all places and ages were bound to sell their estates, and give away the money in charity. For St. Paul's epistles, after this, often speak of the distinction of rich and poor, and Christ hath said that <hi type="italic">the poor we always have with us,</hi> and shall have, and the rich must be always doing them good out of the rents, issues, and profits, of their estates, which they disable themselves to do, if they sell them, and give all away at once. But here the case was extraordinary (1.) They were under no obligation of a divine command to do this, as appears by what Peter said to Ananias (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.4">ch. v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Was it not in thine own power?</hi> But it was a very commendable instance of their raisedness above the world, their contempt of it, their assurance of another world, their love to their brethren, their compassion to the poor, and their great zeal for the encouraging of Christianity, and the nursing of it in its infancy. The apostles left all to follow Christ, and were to give themselves wholly to the word and prayer, and something must be done for their maintenance; so that this extraordinary liberality was like that of Israel in the wilderness towards the building of the tabernacle, which needed to be restrained, <reference osisRef="Exod.36.5-Exod.36.6">Exod. xxxvi. 5, 6</reference>. Our rule is, to give according as God has blessed us; yet, in such an extraordinary case as this, those are to be praised who give <hi type="italic">beyond their power,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.3">2 Cor. viii. 3</reference>. (2.) They were Jews that did this, and those who believed Christ must believe that the Jewish nation would shortly be destroyed, and an end put to the possession of estates and goods in it, and, in the belief of this, they sold them for the present service of Christ and his church. <div eID="gen28980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28981" type="x-p"/> III. God owned them, and gave them signal tokens of his presence with them (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.43">v. 43</reference>): <hi type="italic">Many wonders and signs were done by the apostles</hi> of divers sorts, which confirmed their doctrine, and incontestably proved that it was from God. Those that could work miracles could have maintained themselves and the poor that were among them miraculously, as Christ fed thousands with a little food; but it was as much for the glory of God that it should be done by a miracle of grace (inclining people to sell their estates, to do it) as if it had been done by a miracle in nature. <div eID="gen28981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28982" type="x-p"/> But the Lord's giving them power to work miracles was not all he did for them; he <hi type="italic">added to the church daily.</hi> The word in their mouths <hi type="italic">did wonders,</hi> and God blessed their endeavours for the increase of the number of believers. Note, It is God's work to add souls to the church; and it is a great comfort both to ministers and Christians to see it. <div eID="gen28982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28983" type="x-p"/> IV. The people were influenced by it; those that were without, the standers by, that were spectators. 1. They <hi type="italic">feared them,</hi> and had a veneration for them (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.43">v. 43</reference>): <hi type="italic">Fear came upon every soul,</hi> that is, upon very many who saw the <hi type="italic">wonders</hi> and <hi type="italic">signs</hi> done by the apostles, and were afraid lest their not being respected as they should be would bring desolation upon their nation. The common people stood in awe of them, as Herod feared John. Though they had nothing of external pomp to command external respect, as the <hi type="italic">scribes' long robes</hi> gained them the <hi type="italic">greetings in the market-places,</hi> yet they had abundance of spiritual gifts that were truly honourable, which possessed men with an inward reverence for them. Fear came upon <hi type="italic">every soul;</hi> the <hi type="italic">souls</hi> of people were strangely influenced by their awful preaching and living. 2. They <hi type="italic">favoured them.</hi> Though we have reason to think there were those that despised them and hated them (we are sure the Pharisees and chief priests did), yet far the greater part of the common people had a kindness for them—they <hi type="italic">had favour with all the people.</hi> Christ was so violently run upon and run down by a <hi type="italic">packed mob,</hi> which cried, <hi type="italic">Crucify him, crucify him,</hi> that one would think his doctrine and followers were never likely to have an interest in the common people any more. And yet here we find them <hi type="italic">in favour with them all,</hi> by which it appears that their prosecuting Christ was a sort of force put upon them by the artifices of the priests; now they returned to their wits, to their right mind. Note, Undissembled piety and charity will command respect; and cheerfulness in serving God will recommend religion to those that are without. Some read it, <hi type="italic">They had charity to all the people</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">charin echontes pros holon ton laon</hi></hi>; they did not confine their charity to those of their own community, but it was <hi type="italic">catholic</hi> and <hi type="italic">extensive;</hi> and this recommended them very much. 3. They <hi type="italic">fell over</hi> to them. Some or other were daily coming in, though not so many as the first day; and they were such as <hi type="italic">should be saved.</hi> Note, Those that God has designed for eternal salvation shall one time or other be effectually brought to Christ: and those that are brought to Christ are <hi type="italic">added to the church</hi> in a holy covenant by baptism, and in holy communion by other ordinances.  <chapter eID="Acts.2"/> <div eID="gen28983" type="x-p"/>

entries.0e660f9f0a35a71bdd9bd5c7b91d22aff280749f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15552"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Acts.2.1-Acts.2.13">Ac 2:1-13</reference>. Descent of the Spirit--The Disciples Speak with Tongues--Amazement of the Multitude.</title> <div sID="gen29978" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15552"/><hi type="bold">1-4. when the day of Pentecost was fully come--</hi>The fiftieth from the morrow after the first Passover sabbath (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.15">Le 23:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen29978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29979" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with one accord--</hi>the solemnity of the day, perhaps, unconsciously raising their expectations. <div eID="gen29979" type="x-p"/>
entries.d3f58b2a70a5cc92725a2c8042f0354c2b76d102: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15556"/><div sID="gen29983" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15556"/><hi type="bold">5-11. there were dwelling at Jerusalem Jews, devout men out of every nation--</hi>not, it would seem, permanently settled there (see <reference osisRef="Acts.2.9">Ac 2:9</reference>), though the language seems to imply more than a temporary visit to keep this one feast. <div eID="gen29983" type="x-p"/>
entries.722b57201dfd45050b977f494edcab39d27e2d2f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15558"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Acts.2.14-Acts.2.36">Ac 2:14-36</reference>. Peter for the First Time, Publicly Preaches Christ.</title> <div sID="gen29985" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15558"/><hi type="bold">14-21. Peter, standing up with the eleven--</hi>in advance, perhaps, of the rest. <div eID="gen29985" type="x-p"/>
entries.5389074d863bfe6773524532b425876d13a7d09b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15563"/><div sID="gen29995" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15563"/><hi type="bold">22-28. a man approved of God--</hi>rather, "authenticated," "proved," or "demonstrated to be from God."<div eID="gen29995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29996" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by miracles ... which God did by him--</hi>This is not a low view of our Lord's miracles, as has been alleged, nor inconsistent with <reference osisRef="John.2.11">Joh 2:11</reference>, but is in strict accordance with His progress from humiliation to glory, and with His own words in <reference osisRef="John.5.19">Joh 5:19</reference>. This view of Christ is here dwelt on to exhibit to the Jews the whole course of Jesus of Nazareth as the ordinance and doing of the God of Israel [Alford]. <div eID="gen29996" type="x-p"/>
entries.4416816b804ccb8940277fb8567f0614ac65c6d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15568"/><div sID="gen30004" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15568"/><hi type="bold">29-36. David ... is ... dead and buried, &c.--</hi>Peter, full of the Holy Ghost, sees in this sixteenth Psalm, one Holy Man, whose life of high devotedness and lofty spirituality is crowned with the assurance, that though He taste of death, He shall rise again without seeing corruption, and be admitted to the bliss of God's immediate presence. Now as this was palpably untrue of David, it could be meant only of One other, even of Him whom David was taught to expect as the final Occupant of the throne of Israel. (Those, therefore, and they are many, who take David himself to be the subject of this Psalm, and the words quoted to refer to Christ only in a more eminent sense, nullify the whole argument of the apostle). The Psalm is then affirmed to have had its only proper fulfilment in Jesus, of whose resurrection and ascension they were witnesses, while the glorious effusion of the Spirit by the hand of the ascended One, setting an infallible seal upon all, was even then witnessed by the thousands who stood listening to Him. A further illustration of Messiah's ascension and session at God's right hand is drawn from <reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Psa 110:1</reference>, in which David cannot be thought to speak of himself, seeing he is still in his grave. <div eID="gen30004" type="x-p"/>
entries.10e79b1d3d9e5029e11a2e6bc1f86a7bece4aade: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15570"/><div sID="gen30010" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15570"/><hi type="bold">37-40. pricked in their hearts--</hi>the begun fulfilment of <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zec 12:10</reference>, whose full accomplishment is reserved for the day when "all Israel shall be saved" (see on <reference osisRef="Rom.11.26">Ro 11:26</reference>).<div eID="gen30010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30011" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what shall we do?--</hi>This is that beautiful spirit of genuine compunction and childlike docility, which, discovering its whole past career to have been one frightful mistake, seeks only to be set right for the future, be the change involved and the sacrifices required what they may. So Saul of Tarsus (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.6">Ac 9:6</reference>). <div eID="gen30011" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b169fd6800872a265f7ab5ee8321e37da50dea0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15574"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Acts.2.41-Acts.2.47">Ac 2:41-47</reference>. Beautiful Beginnings of the Christian Church.</title> <div sID="gen30018" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15574"/><hi type="bold">41-47. they that gladly received his word were baptized--</hi>"It is difficult to say how three thousand could be baptized in one day, according to the old practice of a complete submersion; and the more as in Jerusalem there was no water at hand except Kidron and a few pools. The difficulty can only be removed by supposing that they already employed sprinkling, or baptized in houses in large vessels. Formal submersion in rivers, or larger quantities of water, probably took place only where the locality conveniently allowed it" [Olshausen].<div eID="gen30018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30019" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the same day there were added to them about three thousand souls--</hi>fitting inauguration of the new kingdom, as an economy of the Spirit! <div eID="gen30019" type="x-p"/>

entries.e9b6561ed74710855ad7d234aa287bdd39571d33: <div eID="gen43312" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen43313" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen43314" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen43314" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen43313" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen43315" type="x-p"/> The day of pentecost being arrived, and the disciples assembled, the Holy Spirit descended as a mighty rushing wind, and in the likeness of fiery tongues sat upon them; in consequence of which, they were all enabled to speak different languages, which they had never learned, <reference osisRef="Act.2.1-Act.2.4">Act 2:1-4</reference>. An account of persons from various countries who there present, and were astonished to hear the apostles declare the wonderful works of God in their respective languages, <reference osisRef="Act.2.5-Act.2.12">Act 2:5-12</reference>. Some cavil, <reference osisRef="Act.2.13">Act 2:13</reference>, and are confounded by Peter, who asserts that this work is of God; and that thereby a most important prophecy was fulfilled, <reference osisRef="Act.2.14-Act.2.21">Act 2:14-21</reference>. He takes occasion from this to preach Jesus to them, as the true Lord and only Messiah, <reference osisRef="Act.2.22-Act.2.36">Act 2:22-36</reference>. The people are alarmed and convinced, and inquire what they shall do, <reference osisRef="Act.2.37">Act 2:37</reference>. He exhorts them to repent and be baptized in the name of Jesus, that they may receive remission of sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit, <reference osisRef="Act.2.38-Act.2.40">Act 2:38-40</reference>. They gladly receive his word, about three thousand are baptized and added to the Church in one day; they continue steadfast in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, <reference osisRef="Act.2.41">Act 2:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.2.42">Act 2:42</reference>. The apostles work many miracles; and the disciples have all things in common, and live in a state of great happiness and Christian fellowship, <reference osisRef="Act.2.43-Act.2.47">Act 2:43-47</reference>. <div eID="gen43315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43316" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen43316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43317" type="x-p"/> When the day of pentecost was fully come - The feast of pentecost was celebrated fifty days after the passover, and has its name πεντηκοστη from πεντηκοντα, fifty, which is compounded of πεντε, five, and ηκοντα, the decimal termination. It commenced on the fiftieth day reckoned from the first day of unleavened bread, i.e. on the morrow after the paschal lamb was offered. The law relative to this feast is found in <reference osisRef="Lev.23.15">Lev 23:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.16">Lev 23:16</reference>, in these words: And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the Sabbath, from the day that ye brought the sheaf of the wave-offering; seven Sabbaths shall be complete: even unto the morrow after the seventh Sabbath shall ye number fifty days. This feast was instituted in commemoration of the giving the law on Mount Sinai; and is therefore sometimes called by the Jews, שמחת תורה shimchath torah, the joy of the law, and frequently the feast of weeks. There is a correspondence between the giving of the law, which is celebrated by this feast of pentecost, together with the crucifixion of our Lord, which took place at the passover, and this descent of the Holy Spirit, which happened at this pentecost. <div eID="gen43317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43318" type="x-p"/> 1. At the passover, the Israelites were delivered from Egyptian bondage: this was a type of the thraldom in which the human race were to Satan and sin. <div eID="gen43318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43319" type="x-p"/> 2. At the passover Jesus Christ, who was typified by the paschal lamb, was sacrificed for the sin of the world, and by this sacrifice redemption from sin and Satan is now procured and proclaimed. <div eID="gen43319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43320" type="x-p"/> 3. On the pentecost, God gave his law on Mount Sinai, accompanied with thunderings and lightnings. On the pentecost, God sent down his Holy Spirit, like a rushing mighty wind; and tongues of fire sat upon each disciple, in order that, by his influence, that new law of light and life might be promulgated and established. Thus, the analogy between the Egyptian bondage and the thraldom occasioned by sin - the deliverance from Egypt, and the redemption from sin - the giving of the law, with all its emblematic accompaniments, and the sending down the Holy Spirit, with its symbols of light, life, and power, has been exactly preserved. <div eID="gen43320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43321" type="x-p"/> 4. At the Jewish passover, Christ was degraded, humbled, and ignominiously put to death: at the following festival, the pentecost, he was highly glorified; and the all conquering and ever during might of his kingdom then commenced. The Holy Spirit seems to have designed all these analogies, to show that, through all preceding ages, God had the dispensation of the Gospel continually in view; and that the old law and its ordinances were only designed as preparatives for the new. <div eID="gen43321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43322" type="x-p"/> They were all with one accord in one place - It is probable that the All here mentioned means the one hundred and twenty spoken of <reference osisRef="Act.1.15">Act 1:15</reference>, who were all together at the election of Matthias. With one accord, ὁμοθυμαδον; this word is very expressive: it signifies that all their minds, affections, desires, and wishes, were concentred in one object, every man having the same end in view; and, having but one desire, they had but one prayer to God, and every heart uttered it. There was no person uninterested - none unconcerned - none lukewarm; all were in earnest; and the Spirit of God came down to meet their united faith and prayer. When any assembly of God's people meet in the same spirit they may expect every blessing they need. <div eID="gen43322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43323" type="x-p"/> In one place. - Where this place was we cannot tell: it was probably in the temple, as seems to be intimated in <reference osisRef="Act.2.46">Act 2:46</reference>, where it is said they were daily ὁμοθυμαδον εν τῳ ἱερῳ, with one accord in the temple; and as this was the third hour of the day, <reference osisRef="Act.2.15">Act 2:15</reference>, which was the Jewish hour of morning prayer, as the ninth hour was the hour of evening prayer, <reference osisRef="Act.3.1">Act 3:1</reference>, it is most probable that the temple was the place in which they were assembled.
entries.792eb9956c9e5aff7373f7cbed80402a8685ca99: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen43323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43324" type="x-p"/> A sound from heaven - Probably thunder is meant, which is the harbinger of the Divine presence. <div eID="gen43324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43325" type="x-p"/> Rushing mighty wind - The passage of a large portion of electrical fluid over that place would not only occasion the sound, or thunder, but also the rushing mighty wind; as the air would rush suddenly and strongly into the vacuum occasioned by the rarefaction of the atmosphere in that place, through the sudden passage of the electrical fluid; and the wind would follow the direction of the fire. There is a good deal of similarity between this account and that of the appearance of God to Elijah, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.11">1Kgs 19:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.12">1Kgs 19:12</reference>, where the strong wind, the earthquake, and the fire, were harbingers of the Almighty's presence, and prepared the heart of Elijah to hear the small still voice; so, this sound, and the mighty rushing wind, prepared the apostles to receive the influences and gifts of the Holy Spirit. In both cases, the sound, strong wind, and fire, although natural agents, were supernaturally employed. See the note on <reference osisRef="Act.9.7">Act 9:7</reference>.
entries.114aa0cd2d302c281d36edfbf5ac2bb5936ddef7: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen43325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43326" type="x-p"/> Cloven tongues like as of fire - The tongues were the emblem of the languages they were to speak. The cloven tongues pointed out the diversity of those languages; and the fire seemed to intimate that the whole would be a spiritual gift, and be the means of bringing light and life to the souls who should hear them preach the everlasting Gospel in those languages. <div eID="gen43326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43327" type="x-p"/> Sat upon each of them - Scintillations, coruscations, or flashes of fire, were probably at first frequent through every part of the room where they were sitting; at last these flashes became defined, and a lambent flame, in the form of a cloven tongue, became stationary on the head of each disciple; a proof that the Spirit of God had made each his temple or residence. That unusual appearances of fire were considered emblems of the presence and influence of God, both the Scriptures and the Jewish writings amply prove. Thus God manifested himself to Moses, when he appointed him to deliver Israel, <reference osisRef="Exo.3.2">Exo 3:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.3.3">Exo 3:3</reference>; and thus he manifested himself when he delivered the law on Mount Sinai, <reference osisRef="Exo.19.16-Exo.19.20">Exo 19:16-20</reference>. The Jews, in order to support the pretensions of their rabbins, as delivering their instructions by Divine authority and influence, represent them as being surrounded with fire while they were delivering their lectures; and that their words, in consequence, penetrated and exhilarated the souls of their disciples. Some of the Mohammedans represent Divine inspiration in the same way. In a fine copy of a Persian work, entitled Ajaceb al Makhlookat, or Wonders of Creation, now before me, where a marred account of Abraham's sacrifice, mentioned <reference osisRef="Gen.15.9-Gen.15.17">Gen 15:9-17</reference>, is given, instead of the burning lamp passing between the divided pieces of the victim, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.17">Gen 15:17</reference>, Abraham is represented standing between four fowls, the cock, the peacock, the duck, and the crow, with his head almost wrapped in a flame of lambent fire, as the emblem of the Divine communication made to him of the future prosperity of his descendants. The painting in which this is represented is most exquisitely finished. This notion of the manner in which Divine intimations were given was not peculiar to the Jews and Arabians; it exists in all countries; and the glories which appear round the heads of Chinese, Hindoo, and Christian saints, real or supposed, were simply intended to signify that they had especial intercourse with God, and that his Spirit, under the emblem of fire, sat upon them and became resident in them. There are numerous proofs of this in several Chinese and Hindoo paintings in my possession; and how frequently this is to be met with in legends, missals, and in the ancient ecclesiastical books of the different Christian nations of Europe, every reader acquainted with ecclesiastical antiquity knows well. See the dedication of Solomon's temple, <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.1-2Chr.7.3">2Chr 7:1-3</reference>. <div eID="gen43327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43328" type="x-p"/> The Greek and Roman heathens had similar notions of the manner in which Divine communications were given: strong wind, loud and repeated peals of thunder, coruscations of lightning, and lambent flames resting on those who were objects of the Deities regard, are all employed by them to point out the mode in which their gods were reported to make their will known to their votaries. Every thing of this kind was probably borrowed from the account given by Moses of the appearance on Mount Sinai; for traditions of this event were carried through almost every part of the habitable world, partly by the expelled Canaanites, partly by the Greek sages travelling through Asiatic countries in quest of philosophic truth: and partly by means of the Greek version of the Septuagint, made nearly three hundred years before the Christian era. "A flame of fire seen upon the head of any person was, among the heathens, considered as an omen from their gods that the person was under the peculiar care of a supernatural power, and destined to some extraordinary employment. Many proofs of this occur in the Roman poets and historians. Wetstein, in his note on this place, has made an extensive collection of them. I shall quote but one, which almost every reader of the Aeneid of Virgil will recollect: - <div eID="gen43328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43329" type="x-p"/> Talia vociferans gemitu tectum omne replebat: <div eID="gen43329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43330" type="x-p"/> Cum subitum, dictuque oritur mirabile monstrum. <div eID="gen43330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43331" type="x-p"/> Namque manus inter, maestorumque ora parentum. <div eID="gen43331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43332" type="x-p"/> Ecce levis summo de vertice visus <div eID="gen43332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43333" type="x-p"/> Iuli Fundere lumen apex, tactuque innoxia molli <div eID="gen43333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43334" type="x-p"/> Lambere flamma comas, et circum tempora pasci. <div eID="gen43334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43335" type="x-p"/> Nos pavidi trepidare metu, crinemque flagrantem <div eID="gen43335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43336" type="x-p"/> Excutere, et sanctos restinguere fontibus ignes. <div eID="gen43336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43337" type="x-p"/> At pater Anchises oculos ad sidera laetus <div eID="gen43337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43338" type="x-p"/> Extulit, et coelo palamas cum voce tetendit: <div eID="gen43338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43339" type="x-p"/> Jupiter omnipotens - <div eID="gen43339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43340" type="x-p"/> Da auxilium, pater, atque haec omina firma. <div eID="gen43340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43341" type="x-p"/> Virg. Aen. ii. v. 679. <div eID="gen43341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43342" type="x-p"/> While thus she fills the house with clamorous cries, <div eID="gen43342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43343" type="x-p"/> Our hearing is diverted by our eyes; <div eID="gen43343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43344" type="x-p"/> For while I held my son, in the short space <div eID="gen43344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43345" type="x-p"/> Betwixt our kisses and our last embrace, <div eID="gen43345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43346" type="x-p"/> Strange to relate! from young Iulus' head, <div eID="gen43346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43347" type="x-p"/> A lambent flame arose, which gently spread <div eID="gen43347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43348" type="x-p"/> Around his brows, and on his temples fed. <div eID="gen43348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43349" type="x-p"/> Amazed, with running water, we prepare <div eID="gen43349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43350" type="x-p"/> To quench the sacred fire, and slake his hair; <div eID="gen43350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43351" type="x-p"/> But old Anchises, versed in omens, rear'd <div eID="gen43351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43352" type="x-p"/> His hands to heaven, and this request preferr'd: <div eID="gen43352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43353" type="x-p"/> If any vows almighty Jove can bend, <div eID="gen43353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43354" type="x-p"/> Confirm the glad presage which thou art pleased to send. <div eID="gen43354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43355" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen43355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43356" type="x-p"/> There is nothing in this poetic fiction which could be borrowed from our sacred volume; as Virgil died about twenty years before the birth of Christ. <div eID="gen43356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43357" type="x-p"/> It may be just necessary to observe, that tongue of fire may be a Hebraism: for in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.24">Isa 5:24</reference>, לשון אש leshon esh, which we render simply fire, is literally a tongue of fire, as the margin very properly has it. The Hebrews give the name of tongue to most things which terminate in a blunt point: so a bay is termed in <reference osisRef="Jos.15.2">Jos 15:2</reference>, לשן lashon, a tongue. And in <reference osisRef="Jos.15.5">Jos 15:5</reference>, what appears to have been a promontory is called לשון הים leshon hayam, a tongue of the sea. <div eID="gen43357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43358" type="x-p"/> It sat upon each - That is, one of those tongues, like flames, sat upon the head of each disciple; and the continuance of the appearance, which is indicated by the word sat, shows that there could be no illusion in the case. I still think that in all this case the agent was natural, but supernaturally employed.
entries.538e7cc0fddf92a0f96b60f6050fd9d0c5d9b1f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen43358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43359" type="x-p"/> To speak with other tongues - At the building of Babel the language of the people was confounded; and, in consequence of this, they became scattered over the face of the earth: at this foundation of the Christian Church, the gift of various languages was given to the apostles, that the scattered nations might be gathered; and united under one shepherd and superintendent (επισκοπος) of all souls. <div eID="gen43359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43360" type="x-p"/> As the Spirit gave them utterance - The word αποφθεγγεσθαι seems to imply such utterance as proceeded from immediate inspiration, and included oracular communications.
entries.d7273236e21b3bbe731ae958a2314f8b1122ea5f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen43360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43361" type="x-p"/> Devout men, out of every nation - Either by these we are simply to understand Jews who were born in different countries, and had now come up to Jerusalem to be present at the passover, and for purposes of traffic, or proselytes to Judaism, who had come up for the same purpose: for I cannot suppose that the term ανδρες ευλαβεις, devout men, can be applied to any other. At this time there was scarcely a commercial nation under heaven where the Jews had not been scattered for the purpose of trade, merchandize, etc., and from all these nations, it is said, there were persons now present at Jerusalem.
entries.aa2d350c2d0f6d4599f969bc5e41678a828595c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen43361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43362" type="x-p"/> When this was noised abroad - If we suppose that there was a considerable peal of thunder, which followed the escape of a vast quantity of electric fluid, and produced the mighty rushing wind already noticed on <reference osisRef="Act.2.2">Act 2:2</reference>, then the whole city must have been alarmed; and, as various circumstances might direct their attention to the temple, having flocked thither they were farther astonished and confounded to hear the disciples of Christ addressing the mixed multitude in the languages of the different countries from which these people had come. <div eID="gen43362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43363" type="x-p"/> Every man heard them speak in his own language - Use may naturally suppose that, as soon as any person presented himself to one of these disciples, he, the disciple, was immediately enabled to address him in his own language, however various this had been from the Jewish or Galilean dialects. If a Roman presented himself, the disciple was immediately enabled to address him in Latin - if a Grecian, in Greek - an Arab, in Arabic, and so of the rest.
entries.07739cba3e47a8c9fc7e53fb30e78c71302d08e0: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen43363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43364" type="x-p"/> Are not all these - Galileans? - Persons who know no other dialect, save that of their own country. Persons wholly uneducated, and, consequently, naturally ignorant of those languages which they now speak so fluently.
entries.43aedec9bbba2485c81927e2c075421c48695600: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen43364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43365" type="x-p"/> How hear we every man in our own tongue - Some have supposed from this that the miracle was not so much wrought on the disciples as on their hearers: imagining that, although the disciples spoke their own tongue, yet every man so understood what was spoken as if it had been spoken in the language in which he was born. Though this is by no means so likely as the opinion which states that the disciples themselves spoke all these different languages, yet the miracle is the same, howsoever it be taken; for it must require as much of the miraculous power of God to enable an Arab to understand a Galilean, as to enable a Galilean to speak Arabic. But that the gift of tongues was actually given to the apostles, we have the fullest proof; as we find particular ordinances laid down by those very apostles for the regulation of the exercise of this gift; see <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.1">1Cor 14:1</reference>, etc.
entries.9af7c65c943a6e14e473c2bf08adc21d9b920adc: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen43365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43366" type="x-p"/> Parthians - Parthia anciently included the northern part of modern Persia: it was situated between the Caspian Sea and Persian Gulf, rather to the eastward of both. <div eID="gen43366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43367" type="x-p"/> Medes - Media was a country lying in the vicinity of the Caspian Sea; having Parthia on the east, Assyria on the south, and Mesopotamia on the west. <div eID="gen43367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43368" type="x-p"/> Elamites - Probably inhabitants of that country now called Persia: both the Medes and Elamites were a neighboring people, dwelling beyond the Tigris. <div eID="gen43368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43369" type="x-p"/> Mesopotamia - Now Diarbec in Asiatic Turkey; situated between the rivers Tigris and Euphrates; having Assyria on the east, Arabia Deserta with Babylonia on the south, Syria on the west, and Armenia on the north. It was called Padan-aram by the ancient Hebrews, and by the Asiatics is now called Maverannhar, i.e. the country beyond the river. <div eID="gen43369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43370" type="x-p"/> Judea - This word has exceedingly puzzled commentators and critics; and most suspect that it is not the true reading. Bishop Pearce supposes that Ιουδαιαν is an adjective, agreeing with Μεσοποταμιαν, and translates the passage thus: the dwellers in Jewish Mesopotamia. He vindicates this translation by showing that great numbers of the Jews were settled in this country: Josephus says that the ten tribes remained in this country till his time; that "there were countless myriads of them there, and that it was impossible to know their numbers." - Μυριαδες απειροι, και αριθμῳ γνωσθηναι μη δυναμεναι. See Ant. lib. xv. c. 2, s. 2, and c. 3, s. 1; Bell. Jud. lib. i. c. 1, 2. This interpretation, however ingenious, does not comport with the present Greek text. Some imagine that Ιουδαιαν is not the original reading; and therefore they have corrected it into Syriam, Syria; Armeniam, Armenia; Ινδιαν, India; Λυδιαν, Lydia; Ιδουμαιαν, Idumea; Βιθυνιαν, Bithynia; and Κιλικιαν, Cilicia: all these stand on very slender authority, as may be seen in Griesbach; and the last is a mere conjecture of Dr. Mangey. If Judea be still considered the genuine reading, we may account for it thus: the men who were speaking were known to be Galileans; now the Galilean dialect was certainly different from that spoken in Judea - the surprise was occasioned by a Jew being able to comprehend the speech of a Galilean, without any interpreter and without difficulty; and yet it is not easy to suppose that there was such a difference between the two dialects as to render these people wholly unintelligible to each other. <div eID="gen43370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43371" type="x-p"/> Cappadocia - Was an ancient kingdom of Asia comprehending all that country that lies between Mount Taurus and the Euxine Sea. <div eID="gen43371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43372" type="x-p"/> Pontus - Was anciently a very powerful kingdom of Asia, originally a part of Cappadocia; bounded on the east by Colchis; on the west by the river Halys; on the north by the Black Sea; and on the south by Armenia Minor. The famous Mithridates was king of this country; and it was one of the last which the Romans were able to subjugate. <div eID="gen43372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43373" type="x-p"/> Asia - Meaning probably Asia Minor; it was that part of Turkey in Asia now called Natolia.
entries.f90f50f9882737d88cf25e993254249814ee292b: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen43373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43374" type="x-p"/> Phrygia - A country in Asia Minor, southward of Pontus. <div eID="gen43374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43375" type="x-p"/> Pamphylia - The ancient name of the country of Natolia, now called Caramania, between Lycia and Cilicia, near the Mediterranean Sea. <div eID="gen43375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43376" type="x-p"/> Egypt - A very extensive country of African bounded by the Mediterranean on the north; by the Red Sea and the Isthmus of Suez, which divide it from Arabia, on the east; by Abyssinia or Ethiopia on the south; and by the deserts of Barca and Nubia on the west. It was called Mizraim by the ancient Hebrews, and now Mesr by the Arabians. It extends 600 miles from north to south; and from 100 to 250 in breadth, from east to west. <div eID="gen43376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43377" type="x-p"/> Libya - In a general way, among the Greeks, signified Africa; but the northern part, in the vicinity of Cyrene, is here meant. <div eID="gen43377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43378" type="x-p"/> Cyrene - A country in Africa on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea, southward of the most western point of the Island of Crete. <div eID="gen43378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43379" type="x-p"/> Strangers of Rome - Persons dwelling at Rome, and speaking the Latin language, partly consisting of regularly descended Jews and proselytes to the Jewish religion.
entries.39c7811bed413ff1909d12697f25c2c0cdb24d87: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen43379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43380" type="x-p"/> Cretes - Natives of Crete, a large and noted island in the Levant, or eastern part of the Mediterranean Sea, now called Candia. <div eID="gen43380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43381" type="x-p"/> Arabians - Natives of Arabia, a well known country of Asia, having the Red Sea on the west; the Persian Gulf on the east; Judea on the north; and the Indian Ocean on the south. <div eID="gen43381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43382" type="x-p"/> The wonderful works of God - Such as the incarnation of Christ; his various miracles, preaching, death, resurrection, and ascension; and the design of God to save the world through him. From this one circumstance we may learn that all the people enumerated above were either Jews or proselytes; and that there was probably none that could be, strictly speaking, called heathens among them. It may at first appear strange that there could be found Jews in so many different countries, some of which were very remote from the others; but there is a passage in Philo's Embassy to Caius which throws considerable light on the subject. In a letter sent to Caius by King Agrippa, he speaks of to the holy city of Jerusalem, not merely as the metropolis of Judea, but of many other regions, because of the colonies at different times led out of Judea, not only into neighboring countries, such as Egypt, Phoenicia, Syria, and Coelosyria, but also into those that are remote, such as Pamphylia, Cilicia, and the chief parts of Asia as far as Bithynia, and the innermost parts of Pontus; also in the regions of Europe, Thessaly, Boeotia, Macedonia, Aetolia, Attica, Argos, Corinth, and the principal parts of Peloponnesus. Not only the continents and provinces (says he) are full of Jewish colonies, but the most celebrated isles also, Euboea, Cyprus, and Crete, not to mention the countries beyond the Euphrates. All these (a small part of Babylon and some other praefectures excepted, which possess fertile territories) are inhabited by Jews. Not only my native city entreats thy clemency, but other cities also, situated in different parts of the world, Asia, Europe, Africa; both islands, sea coasts, and inland countries." Philonis Opera, edit. Mangey, vol. ii. p. 587. <div eID="gen43382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43383" type="x-p"/> It is worthy of remark that almost all the places and provinces mentioned by St. Luke are mentioned also in this letter of King Agrippa. These, being all Jews or proselytes, could understand in some measure the wonderful works of God, of which mere heathens could have formed no conception. It was wisely ordered that the miraculous descent of the Holy Ghost should take place at this time, when so many from various nations were present to bear witness to what was done, and to be themselves subjects of his mighty working. These, on their return to their respective countries, would naturally proclaim what things they saw and heard; and by this the way of the apostles was made plain; and thus Christianity made a rapid progress over all those parts in a very short time after the resurrection of our Lord.
entries.595254863d4c9195cbd0e1e045bd765db97647b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen43383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43384" type="x-p"/> These men are full of new wine - Rather sweet wine, for γλευκους, cannot mean the mustum, or new wine, as there could be none in Judea so early as pentecost. The Γλευκος, gleucus, seems to have been a peculiar kind of wine, and is thus described by Hesychius and Suidas: Γλευκος, το αποσταγμα της σταφυλης, πριν πατηθῃ. Gleucus is that which distils from the grape before it is pressed. This must be at once both the strongest and sweetest wine. Calmet observes that the ancients had the secret of preserving wine sweet through the whole year, and were fond of taking morning draughts of it: to this Horace appears to refer, Sat. l. ii. s. iv. ver. 24. <div eID="gen43384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43385" type="x-p"/> Aufidius forti miscebat mella Falerno. <div eID="gen43385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43386" type="x-p"/> Mendose: quoniam vacuis committere venis <div eID="gen43386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43387" type="x-p"/> Nil nisi lene decet: leni praecordia mulso <div eID="gen43387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43388" type="x-p"/> Prolueris melius. <div eID="gen43388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43389" type="x-p"/> Aufidius first, most injudicious, quaffed <div eID="gen43389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43390" type="x-p"/> Strong wine and honey for his morning draught. <div eID="gen43390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43391" type="x-p"/> With lenient bev'rage fill your empty veins, <div eID="gen43391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43392" type="x-p"/> For lenient must will better cleanse the reins. <div eID="gen43392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43393" type="x-p"/> Francis.
entries.1c328a869b40ab1af98e6e478293c8ca135e95f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen43393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43394" type="x-p"/> Peter, standing up with the eleven - They probably spoke by turns, not altogether; but Peter began the discourse. <div eID="gen43394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43395" type="x-p"/> All ye that dwell at Jerusalem - Οἱ κατοικουντες would be better translated by the word sojourn, because these were not inhabitants of Judea, but the strangers mentioned in <reference osisRef="Act.2.9-Act.2.11">Act 2:9-11</reference>, who had come up to the feast.
entries.82aae1f75fbd1547ed97246a83dbe5aef086dd6b: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen43395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43396" type="x-p"/> But the third hour of the day - That is, about nine o'clock in the morning, previously to which the Jews scarcely ever ate or drank, for that hour was the hour of prayer. This custom appears to have been so common that even the most intemperate among the Jews were not known to transgress it; Peter therefore spoke with confidence when he said, these are not drunken - seeing it is but the third hour of the day, previously to which even the intemperate did not use wine.
entries.5bbb0013fbb736ce8ec48fae0dbc11f78693ea37: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen43396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43397" type="x-p"/> Spoken by the prophet Joel - The prophecy which he delivered so long ago is just now fulfilled; and this is another proof that Jesus whom ye have crucified is the Messiah.
entries.5578cf96b04e74f837bdf0b279ea33393332d1ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen43397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43398" type="x-p"/> In the last days - The time of the Messiah; and so the phrase was understood among the Jews. <div eID="gen43398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43399" type="x-p"/> I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh - Rabbi Tanchum says, "When Moses laid his hands upon Joshua, the holy blessed God said, In the time of the old text, each individual prophet prophesied; but, in the times of the Messiah, all the Israelites shall be prophets." And this they build on the prophecy quoted in this place by Peter. <div eID="gen43399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43400" type="x-p"/> Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy - The word prophesy is not to be understood here as implying the knowledge and discovery of future events; but signifies to teach and proclaim the great truths of God, especially those which concerned redemption by Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen43400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43401" type="x-p"/> Your young men shall see visions, etc. - These were two of the various ways in which God revealed himself under the Old Testament. Sometimes he revealed himself by a symbol, which was a sufficient proof of the Divine presence: fire was the most ordinary, as it was the most expressive, symbol. Thus he appeared to Moses on Mount Horeb, and afterwards at Sinai; to Abraham, Genesis 15:1-21; to Elijah, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.11">1Kgs 19:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.12">1Kgs 19:12</reference>. At other times he revealed himself by angelic ministry: this was frequent, especially in the days of the patriarchs, of which we find many instances in the book of Genesis. <div eID="gen43401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43402" type="x-p"/> By dreams he discovered his will in numerous instances: see the remarkable case of Joseph, <reference osisRef="Gen.37.5">Gen 37:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.37.9">Gen 37:9</reference>; of Jacob, <reference osisRef="Gen.28.1">Gen 28:1</reference>, etc.; <reference osisRef="Gen.46.2">Gen 46:2</reference>, etc.; of Pharaoh, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.1-Gen.41.7">Gen 41:1-7</reference>; of Nebuchadnezzar, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.10-Dan.4.17">Dan 4:10-17</reference>. For the different ways in which God communicated the knowledge of his will to mankind, see the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.15.1">Gen 15:1</reference>.
entries.6d87248d80b7b1851f0721f39b3d1d9e302e0eec: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen43402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen43403" type="x-p"/> On my servants and on my handmaidens - This properly means persons of the lowest condition, such as male and female slaves. As the Jews asserted that the spirit of prophecy never rested upon a poor man, these words are quoted to show that, under the Gospel dispensation, neither bond nor free, male nor female, is excluded from sharing in the gifts and graces of the Divine Spirit.
